t: Minimum Number of Food Buckets to Feed the Hamsters: Greedy Bucket Placement
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Buckets may occupy only `'.'` cells and feed exactly the hamsters immediately adjacent to them; every hamster needs at least one adjacent bucket. Minimize the bucket count or return `-1`. In `"H..H"` the two hamsters are too far apart to share, costing 2 buckets; in `".H.H."` a single bucket at index 2 feeds both hamsters, costing 1; in `".HHH."` the middle hamster is boxed in by hamsters on both sides, so even filling every dot fails and the answer is -1. With lengths up to `10^5`, a linear strategy is required.
k: A bucket feeds at most the hamster on each side, so the only economy is sharing one bucket between an H.H pattern.
Greedy left-to-right: when the current hamster is unfed, place its bucket on the RIGHT if possible - that bucket can still feed the next hamster too.
Any hamster whose two neighbors are both hamsters or boundaries (patterns like HHH, HH at an end, or a lone H) makes feeding impossible.

a.i: Process hamsters left to right, tracking which cells hold buckets. If hamster i is already fed by a bucket at i-1, skip it. Otherwise it needs a bucket now: prefer i+1 when it is an empty cell, because that placement can also serve hamster i+2; fall back to i-1 if it is empty; if neither exists, the instance is impossible. Preferring the right side is what makes .H.H. cost 1 instead of 2.
s: Keep a used[] marker for bucket cells.
For each hamster i already fed by a bucket at i-1, continue.
Else place a bucket at i+1 if that cell is empty and in range; count it.
Else place at i-1 if empty; count it. Otherwise return -1.
a.t: O(n) - one pass with constant work per cell

a.n: Approach 2: Feasibility Check Plus Shared-Pair Counting
a.i: Reformulate: every bucket normally serves one hamster; pairing hamsters i and i+2 around a dot saves exactly one bucket, and disjoint pairs form a matching on a path, which the left-to-right greedy maximizes. So the answer is (#hamsters) - (#disjoint H.H pairs), provided the instance is feasible: every hamster needs at least one empty neighbor, i.e. no hamster is squeezed between two hamsters/boundaries. Any paired hamster's dedicated fallback slot stays free, so unmatched hamsters can always be served individually.
s: Feasibility: return -1 if some hamster i has (boundary or H) on both sides.
Scan i left to right: whenever H at i, dot at i+1, H at i+2 and neither hamster is paired yet, mark both paired.

w:
**Wrap-up**

Lead with the greedy placement; the pair-counting identity (answer = hamsters minus disjoint H.H shares) is a nice way to prove optimality or to sanity-check outputs. Pitfalls: preferring the LEFT bucket breaks sharing (`".H.H."` would cost 2 instead of 1), and forgetting boundary hamsters (`"H"`, `"HH"`) must return -1. Edge cases to test: `"H"`, `"HH"`, `"HHH"`, `".H.H."`, `"H..H"`. Follow-up: a circular row changes neighbor logic and needs the same greedy with a wrap-around feasibility check.
